newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Corruption on rise among Russian police - officials.
newsitem.headline: Corruption on rise among Russian police - officials.

text.p: The number of Russian police officers charged with corruption rose sharply last year, but such cases represented only "the tip of the iceberg", Interior Ministry officials said on Thursday.

Police departments across Russia fired 21,347 officers last year for violating internal rules, but just 404 officers were punished on corruption charges, according to Interior Ministry statistics released on Thursday.

"These clearly do not represent all of the acts of corruption and extortion committed by our staff," said Major General Svyatoslav Golitsyn, head of the ministry's internal affairs division. "It's just the tip of the iceberg. I'm sure acts of corruption are far more frequent."
Still, he told a news briefing that the number of criminal cases opened against police for taking bribes has increased sixfold in recent years.
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 and the emergence of a chaotic market system in its wake has created new opportunities for law enforcement officials to earn money illegally on the side.

Many Russians feel they can no longer turn to the once-feared police for protection against the wave of crime that has spread in recent years. Many businesses use organised criminal groups to provide protection and mediate disputes rather than turn to the police.
President Boris Yeltsin has said that organised crime and corruption threaten the very existence of the state and has launched a high-profile campaign against graft.
Recent cases against police, where servicemen's average salary is about $100 a month, show a range of illicit schemes, Golitsyn said.
One police officer in northern Archangelsk region gathered compromising information on tape about citizens and then extorted money to keep quiet.
Another in the Far Eastern Sakhalin region skimmed off funds from earthquake relief donations.
Others used their police connections to operate illegal businesses or to buy state assets at unusually low prices, sometimes easing the way by themselves giving bribes.
The number of criminal cases against traffic police rose 16 percent to 597, with just 83 nabbed for bribery, according to ministry statistics.
Traffic police, who also earn a little more than $100 a month, are widely perceived to be among the most corrupt public sector officials.
Most Russian drivers say they have paid off traffic officers on occasion, and some traffic police acknowledge they must take bribes to supplement their meagre incomes.

Nikolai Borodin, the deputy head of the State Automobile Inspectorate, asked Russian reporters to portray traffic police with more sympathy, and said drivers who give bribes were also breaking the law.
He added that Russia's system of collecting traffic fines is flawed because city governments have no mechanism to collect traffic ticket fines.
